memory_candidates.content: When hand-writing a quick verification snippet (e.g. a shell/awk one-liner) to sanity-check a parser rewrite against a corpus, the snippet must mirror the REAL implementation's classification rules, not just reuse the same regex patterns. A depth-counting marker parser that classifies a line carrying BOTH an open-token and a close-token substring as a net-zero no-op (rather than a pure open, which is what a naive first-match-wins awk snippet checking the open pattern before the close pattern would do) can disagree with that naive snippet on real files. In this task, an ad-hoc balance-trace snippet (copied verbatim from the plan text and reused across five phases) reported a file as balanced throughout implementation, while the REAL shared-library parser -- only exercised when the deployed copy was actually run post-redeploy -- found a genuine stray end hidden in pre-existing header prose. The lesson: verify a parser rewrite's correctness by calling the parser itself (or an equivalent full reimplementation), never a lighter hand-written proxy that shares the old implementation's classification shortcuts.

For a text-marker exemption convention (task-ref-ok style) whose token is matched as a plain substring: when a new test file's fixture data deliberately needs the literal marker substring as byte content fed to the function under test (including deliberately UNBALANCED fixtures, e.g. an unterminated begin or a stray end, which is often the whole point of the test case), compose the token at runtime from concatenated string parts (e.g. tok="marker-name"; MARK_BEGIN="${tok}:begin") rather than writing it as a contiguous literal in the test file's own source. This keeps the new test file's own marker-hygiene trace trivially balanced (zero real occurrences) regardless of what the runtime-constructed strings represent. Separately, any literal citation/payload text the fixture needs (e.g. a task-number-shaped string for a write-time guard's own self-check) should live in its own variable assignment carrying a trailing inline exemption comment on that one line, mirroring the repo's existing convention, rather than embedding it directly in a heredoc body (which would make the heredoc's raw text itself trip the write-time guard scanning the whole new-file payload).
